title: The Count of Traded Wildlife Just Doubled
idea: A new study counts at least 107,356 species used or traded worldwide, more than double the earlier estimate; only a few percent are tracked

scenes.title: The count
scenes.place: A paper ledger on a wooden desk, one huge number written across the page

lines.t: Scientists just counted wildlife for sale. The number doubled.
At least one hundred seven thousand, three hundred fifty-six species.
That is from a study in the journal Science Advances, reported since late October.
Here is what was counted, what was not, and what nobody knows yet.

scenes.title: Before
scenes.place: A wall chart in a quiet office, a small stack of species cards pinned in one corner

lines.t: Until now, the number people used was about fifty thousand species.
It came from a twenty twenty-two assessment by an intergovernmental biodiversity panel called IPBES.
The new study puts the count at more than double that.

scenes.title: What is in it
scenes.place: Three large crates on a loading dock, one marked animals, one plants, one fungi

lines.t: Animals: forty-seven thousand, six hundred eighty-five species.
Plants: at least forty-nine thousand, seven hundred twenty-three, according to the Down To Earth report.
Fungi are counted too. The researchers call it the first global look at how trade in all three is monitored.

scenes.title: Used or traded
scenes.place: Two overlapping circles chalked on a classroom blackboard, one word in each

lines.t: Notice the wording. Used or traded.
A broader count of about sixty thousand plant and fungus species includes uses that are not trade at all.
So that figure is kept apart from the headline number.

scenes.title: Not a doubling of trade
scenes.place: A long table of database folders, a magnifying glass resting on one of them

lines.t: Did trade itself double? The reports do not say that.
This is a new count, put together from many databases. A better count, not a report of more trade.
Each database catches a different slice of the species.

scenes.title: The gaps
scenes.place: A harbour warehouse with shelves of labelled boxes and one empty shelf marked with a question mark

lines.t: Now the gap. Few programmes record trade outside the main treaty list, called CITES, and a few sectors such as fisheries.
Even fewer record whether animals were taken from the wild or bred in captivity.
Or whether the use is sustainable.
Only one country, the United States, systematically records and shares trade data across a wide range of species, the university says.

scenes.title: Watching
scenes.place: A dashboard with a long bar that is almost entirely grey, a thin bright sliver at one end

lines.t: Global biodiversity targets use an indicator to track traded species.
The study estimates that indicator covers about two to three percent of them.
The authors warn that more than ninety-eight percent may fall outside some form of international monitoring.

scenes.title: What is uncertain
scenes.place: A tray of unfinished puzzle pieces beside a half-built picture of a map

lines.t: These are estimates. The team says the real number could be higher, because the data are patchy.
Different outlets round the totals a little differently, so the sources are listed below.

scenes.title: Proposals
scenes.place: A tidy desk with a laptop, a stamped paper permit and a scanner side by side

lines.t: The researchers propose standard ways to record trade, electronic permits instead of paper, and automatic checks of shipping documents.
Those are their recommendations. Nothing here has been decided.

scenes.title: Still unknown
scenes.place: The same ledger on the same wooden desk, the huge number now with a blank line under it

lines.t: Still unknown: how much of this trade is sustainable. The study counts species. It does not say which are in trouble.
If a figure here is out of date, the sources are the reference.
Which gap would you want counted first?
